title: Neural networks and deep learning, in brief
html:
Purpose. Large language models are neural networks, so before the agent chapters you should know the parts. Good news: you already know the first one. A single neuron is a logistic regression.

Key ideas

  • A neuron computes a weighted sum plus a bias, then passes it through an activation function.
  • Layers of neurons learn their own features. Many layers is what "deep" means.
  • Without a non-linear activation, any number of layers collapses into one linear model.
  • Training is gradient descent, with the slopes for all layers computed by backpropagation.
  • For tables of data, trees often win. Neural networks shine on images, text, audio and other unstructured data.

14.1 One neuron

A neuron takes the features, multiplies each by a weight, adds a bias, and applies an activation function g:

a=g(w⃗⋅x⃗+b)a = g(\vec{w} \cdot \vec{x} + b)

With g as the sigmoid this is exactly logistic regression (Chapter 9). Example: inputs x = [2, -1], weights w = [0.5, 0.25], bias b = 0.1. Then z = 2 x 0.5 + (-1) x 0.25 + 0.1 = 0.85. With the ReLU activation (max of 0 and z) the output is 0.85; with the sigmoid it is 0.701.

Activation Formula Where it is used
ReLU max(0, z) the default in hidden layers
Sigmoid 1 / (1 + e^-z) the output for a yes or no
tanh similar to sigmoid, from -1 to 1 older networks, some recurrent ones
Softmax scores turned into probabilities that add to 1 the output for many classes

14.2 Layers learn features

Stack neurons into a layer, and layers into a network. The first layer looks at the raw inputs. The next layer looks at the outputs of the first, and so on. In an image network (Shaw Talebi's example) the first layers detect edges, the next combine edges into eyes and whiskers, and the last decides "cat". Nobody tells the network to look for whiskers: it finds the features that help. This is why deep learning needs far less hand-made feature engineering than the traditional models of Chapter 13 (Chapter 8's feature work is exactly what it automates).

The activation must be non-linear. Two linear layers in a row, W2 (W1 x), equal one linear layer with weights (W2 W1), so without a non-linear function in between, depth adds nothing. The non-linearity is what lets a network learn almost any pattern.

14.3 Training

Training is the gradient descent of Chapter 6 on a cost function, with two additions:

  • Backpropagation computes the slope of the cost with respect to every weight in every layer. It uses the chain rule of calculus: it runs the network forward to get a prediction and the cost, then backward, passing the slopes from the last layer to the first. You do not code this by hand: libraries such as PyTorch do it automatically.
  • Mini-batches and Adam. Each step uses a small batch of examples (8 to 32 in Shaw's example), and the optimizer Adam adapts the step size per parameter (Chapter 6).

The usual hyperparameters are the number of epochs (passes over the data), the learning rate, the batch size and dropout, a regularizer that randomly switches off some neurons during training so that the network cannot rely on any one of them (Chapter 11).

14.4 Architectures

Type Good for Idea
Feed-forward tables, simple tasks layers in a row
Convolutional (CNN) images filters that slide over the picture
Recurrent (RNN, LSTM) sequences a memory carried from step to step
Transformer text, and most modern models attention: every word can look at every other word

A large language model is a very large transformer trained on text to predict the next word. It is trained first on huge amounts of text, then refined with supervised examples and reinforcement learning (Chapter 1).

14.5 When to use it

Use neural networks when the input is unstructured (images, audio, text) and you have a lot of data, or when you can start from a pretrained model, as you will with LLMs and embedding models. For a table of numbers and categories, such as loan data, carefully tuned tree ensembles often match or beat neural networks (Grinsztajn et al. studied this on 45 datasets in Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?). Try the forest first.

Loan example. To read scanned payslips and extract the income, use a neural network (a pretrained vision or language model). To predict whether a customer accepts an offer from a table of 15 columns, start with logistic regression and a gradient-boosted forest.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking "deep" means "better".
  • Training a big network from scratch on a few thousand rows.
  • Forgetting that a network needs the same care as any model: a baseline, scaled inputs, a validation set.

Check yourself

  • Why is logistic regression a one-neuron neural network?
  • Why do hidden layers need a non-linear activation?
  • What does backpropagation compute?
  • You have 5,000 rows of loan data. Do you start with a neural network? Why or why not?
Show answers

(1) A neuron is a weighted sum plus bias passed through an activation; with a sigmoid that is the logistic regression formula. (2) Otherwise stacked layers collapse into a single linear model and add no power. (3) The slope of the cost with respect to every weight, layer by layer, using the chain rule. (4) No: with a small table, start with logistic regression and tree ensembles, which are simpler and usually as accurate; use neural networks for unstructured data or pretrained models.

Go deeper: Shaw Talebi, ML Foundations for AI Engineers · 3Blue1Brown's neural network series (the best visual introduction) · Andrej Karpathy, Neural Networks: Zero to Hero (build one from scratch, then a GPT) · Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, Deep Learning (free, the reference) · Ng's course 2 (neural networks, coming in your plan).
